new_statements.quote: Primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. It is assigned to the word, not the root, therefore stress changes when a root is affixed. vale ['fʒal] 'house' vale-ku [fʒa'lɛŋgu] 'my house' ... In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress occurs on every alternate syllable before the syllable containing primary stress (penultimate syllable). ... The fact that stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable is strong evidence for treating diphthongs as consisting of underlying two vowel sequences, as each vowel must belong to a separate syllable (§2.6.3.1.1).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (underlying, vowel-final) phonological word, counting suffixes and enclitic-bearing forms; stress moves rightward when suffixes are added. Because Lolovoli speech regularly drops word-final vowels (section 2.6.4), the stressed penult often surfaces as a final closed syllable (vale ['Bal], gamali [kha'mal]); word-final surface diphthongs are stressed because they are underlying V.V with stress on the first vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress on every alternate syllable to the left of the primary-stressed penult (e.g. retahi-de [,reta'hinde], lado-lado-gi-ni=e [la,ndola,ndoki'ni]).
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions given. Apparent surface exceptions are derived: word-final diphthongs carry stress (analysed as underlying VV, so still penultimate); word-final vowel deletion in the Lolovoli dialect yields surface final stress on closed syllables; monosyllables always keep their vowel; intensified words lengthen the stressed vowel and release the final vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes (stress 'assigned to the word, not the root'); clitics per section 2.8 do not carry their own stress, and reduplicated forms are re-footed as single words. Statements are about citation/word forms; author notes northern dialects keep final vowels while Lolovoli (south-east) drops them.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyslop 2001 describes the Lolovoli dialect (south-east Ambae) of what she calls the North-East Ambae language = Glottolog east2443 East Ambae [omb]. She notes dialect variation relevant to surface stress: northern dialects of the language keep word-final vowels (consistent CV), whereas Lolovoli drops them in normal speech, so penultimate stress often surfaces word-finally on a closed syllable in Lolovoli but not in the north. Ivens 1940 'Lobaha' is a northern variety of the same language.

sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology, section 2.6.2 'Stress' (p.37): primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (word domain, shifts under suffixation); secondary stress on every alternate syllable leftward in words of 4+ syllables; penultimate regularity used as argument that diphthongs are underlying VV sequences (word-final surface diphthongs carry stress). Section 2.6.4 (pp.39-40): in Lolovoli normal speech word-final vowels are usually dropped, so surface forms often end in a stressed closed syllable, e.g. vale ['Bal] 'house', gamali [kha'mal].
